opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest opportunity is that most of our methods still treat patients as snapshots rather than as trajectories. A typical study takes a scan at diagnosis, maybe a scan after treatment, and compares the two. But a cancer patient's journey generates a huge amount of longitudinal data: repeated imaging, lab values, pathology, treatment changes, symptoms. We tend to collapse all of that into a few summary numbers, and we lose the story of how the disease is actually evolving.

Part of the problem is the data itself. Clinical data collected over time is messy. Scans are taken at irregular intervals, on different machines with different protocols, and patients drop out or switch treatments for reasons that are often related to how they're doing. Many standard machine learning models assume neatly spaced, complete observations, and when you force real-world data into that shape you either throw information away or introduce bias without realizing it.

So I'd like to see more methods that handle irregular sampling and missingness natively, and that model change itself, like how a tumor's texture or shape evolves in imaging, rather than only its state at one point. I'd also like to see more integration across data types, so imaging, genomics, and the clinical record inform each other rather than living in separate silos.

Finally, there's interpretability and generalizability. If a model is going to help an oncologist decide whether to continue a therapy, it needs to explain why it thinks a patient is or isn't responding. And it needs to work at a community hospital, not just at the academic center whose data it was trained on. Getting those pieces right is where I think the real clinical impact will come from.

r001.rationale: The response discusses longitudinal trajectories and how disease evolves, but does not frame time as a fourth dimension.

r002.rationale: It says methods treat patients as snapshots, compare only a few time points, and collapse longitudinal data into summaries, losing how disease evolves.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that most methods still treat a patient as a snapshot, when what we actually have is a story.

Think about what a cancer patient generates over the course of care. There's a baseline CT or MRI, then follow-up scans every few months. There's bloodwork, pathology, genomics, clinical notes, treatment records, maybe patient-reported outcomes. All of that is collected at different times, at irregular intervals, and often for reasons that have nothing to do with research. A scan happens because a clinician was worried about something, not because it was week twelve on a protocol.

The dominant approach has been to pick one time point, usually baseline, and build a model to predict an outcome from it. That throws away the most informative signal we have, which is change. A tumor that's shrinking slowly versus one that's stable versus one that's just starting to grow look very different over time, and that trajectory often tells you more than any single image.

So I'd say there are three places where we need to do better.

The first is handling irregular, missing, and asynchronous data honestly. Many longitudinal methods assume regular sampling, and clinical data simply doesn't look like that. We need models that can take in observations at whatever times they occurred, and that treat the absence of a measurement as potentially informative rather than as noise to be imputed away.

The second is combining modalities over time, not just at one point. Imaging, lab values, and clinical text each evolve on their own schedule. Fusing them at baseline is a solved-ish problem. Fusing their trajectories is not.

The third, and this is the one I care most about, is clinical relevance. A model that predicts survival from the entire history is interesting, but what a clinician really needs is a decision at a specific moment: should we change therapy now, should we bring this person back sooner, is this radiographic change real progression or a treatment effect. That means methods need to be updatable as new data arrives, and they need to tell you something actionable at each visit, with some sense of how confident they are.

There's also a data infrastructure piece underneath all of this. Linking a patient's records across years and systems, and doing it in a way that respects privacy and consent, is unglamorous work. But without it, the modeling advances don't matter, because you can't assemble the longitudinal cohort in the first place.

So room for improvement, yes, quite a lot. But I'd frame it optimistically. The data exists. It's being generated every day in routine care. The gap is in building methods that respect how that data actually arrives and in asking questions clinicians can act on.

r001.rationale: The response emphasizes trajectories and change over time, but does not frame time as a fourth dimension.

r002.rationale: It says many methods use a single baseline snapshot and discard the informative signal of change over time.

astra-6.text: I think there’s a lot of room to improve how we capture change over time. A patient’s cancer isn’t static, but we often analyze their data as though it were—a scan at diagnosis, for example, rather than a sequence of scans showing how the disease responds to treatment. The opportunity is to bring those observations together with treatment history and other clinical information to understand the patient’s trajectory. That’s challenging because patients have different numbers of visits, measurements happen at irregular intervals, and data can be missing. We need methods that account for those realities and help us ask: Is this treatment working, and can we recognize earlier when a different approach might be needed?

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real opportunity to do a better job of capturing how a patient’s disease changes over time. We collect scans, blood tests, and clinical information throughout treatment, but our methods often analyze a single time point or reduce that history to a few measurements. That loses information about the trajectory of the disease and how it responds to treatment.

We need methods that can bring those different sources together while accounting for the fact that patients are measured at different intervals and some data are missing. Ultimately, the goal is to use that evolving picture to help clinicians recognize earlier when a treatment is working or when it might be time to change course.

r001.rationale: The response discusses disease trajectories over time but does not frame time as a fourth dimension.
